name: Flerovium

discovery.discoverer: Yuri Oganessian and team, Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research, notably testing the 'island of stability' hypothesis
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive, though some of its isotopes have unexpectedly longer half-lives (seconds, rather than milliseconds) than neighbouring superheavy elements.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Georgy Flyorov, founder of the Dubna laboratory, and one of the key elements whose surprisingly longer half-lives support the theorized 'island of stability' for certain superheavy nuclei.
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 14 below lead, flerovium's slightly longer-than-expected half-lives are exactly the kind of evidence physicists look for to support the 'island of stability' theory, which predicts certain 'magic number' proton/neutron combinations should resist decay unusually well.
didYouKnow: While most superheavy elements decay in milliseconds, some flerovium isotopes survive for several seconds — a huge relative difference that's seen as tentative evidence for the long-theorized 'island of stability' among superheavy nuclei.
genZNote: Lives noticeably longer than its superheavy neighbours, which is basically the periodic table's version of finding a plot-relevant clue. Island of stability, here we come.
